🖥 Iran Red Crescent urges humanitarian boost in BRICS Civil Council framework

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Iran’s Red Crescent Society (IRSC) has submitted specialized proposals on the Principles of the Framework of the Civil BRICS Council, aimed at strengthening humanitarian dimensions, boosting vulnerable communities’ participation, and leveraging Red Cross/Red Crescent capacities in the council’s structure and activities.

Drawing on its humanitarian missions and wide-ranging operational and social capabilities, the IRSC maintains that attention to humanitarian considerations can make the council’s activities richer in content and more effective, said Razieh Alishvandi, Deputy IRSC Head for International Affairs, on Friday at the second Civil BRICS Council in Russia’s Saint Petersburg.
​
A key focus of the IRSC’s proposals is defining the role of National Red Cross and Red Crescent societies within the membership and participation framework of the Civil BRICS Council, she added.
​
Stressing that affected communities must be heard in BRICS civil decision-making, she said the proposals call for the meaningful participation of people affected by disasters, conflicts, and other humanitarian crises, including women, children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities, with their needs, capacities, and views reflected in policy recommendations while upholding human dignity and the do-no-harm principle.
​
Another proposed focus is adherence to the seven Fundamental Principles of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement: humanity, impartiality, neutrality, independence, voluntary service, unity, and universality, she noted.
​
Referring to the necessity of the Civil BRICS Council’s attention to international humanitarian law, she said: It has been proposed that promoting respect for international humanitarian law, dissemination and education of this law, and providing the ground for dialogue and practical cooperation regarding the protection of civilians and other protected persons in armed conflicts, humanitarian access, protection of humanitarian workers and medical centers, and prevention of attacks against humanitarian workers be placed among the responsibilities of this council.
​
Noting that the Civil BRICS Council must pay attention to international humanitarian law, she said the proposals call for the council to take on responsibilities including promoting respect for and disseminating and teaching international humanitarian law, and fostering dialogue and practical cooperation on protecting civilians and other protected persons in armed conflict, humanitarian access, safeguarding humanitarian workers and medical facilities, and preventing attacks on humanitarian personnel.

🌍 Araghchi: Iran seeks a good, honorable and dignified agreement

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Iran remains open to diplomacy with the United States but will not accept an agreement that compromises its dignity or undermines the victory it has achieved on the battlefield.

In an exclusive interview with Iran Daily , published on Saturday, Araghchi said Tehran was seeking a “good, honorable and dignified agreement,” stressing that any deal must safeguard Iran’s national interests and prevent a renewed conflict.
​
The following is the full text of the interview:
​
“We are seeking an agreement that would ensure there is no more war afterward.” The remark captures Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s approach to the confrontation between Tehran and Washington, as the line between diplomacy and conflict grows increasingly blurred.
​
Araghchi made the comment on his flight back to Tehran this week after visits to Pakistan and Oman. In an interview with Iran Daily, he discussed Tehran’s initiative to end the state of “neither war nor peace”, the US use of blockades and pressure, the prospects for an agreement, Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile and debate over its nuclear doctrine.
​
He described a two-day proposal that followed the compression of an initial seven-day plan. Under it, the United States would fulfill its commitments on the first day, and Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz on the second, when negotiations on a final agreement would begin. Washington did not accept the proposal.
​
Q: What part of Iran’s seven-point proposal was unacceptable to Washington? Was the disagreement over the commitments or their sequence? Was the United States expected to act within 48 hours, with nuclear talks beginning on the third day? If so, why was Washington unwilling to wait even 48 hours for negotiations to begin?
​
We drew up a seven-day plan combining US commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding with new issues, including additional US sanctions and Iran’s demand that they be lifted. The plan, also known as Iran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, contained slightly more than seven requirements. The United States was to fulfill its commitments during the first five or six days. We would reopen the Strait on the sixth day, and negotiations on a final agreement would begin on the seventh. We sent the plan indirectly to the Americans through Qatari intermediaries during our visit to New York in September.
​
For about two months, the intermediaries carried proposals between the two sides. The Americans said they accepted Iran’s demands provided that some of their own requests were added. Those were issues we had agreed to discuss as part of a final agreement. After extensive discussions, one or two US requests were added. As the US elections approached, the intermediaries proposed shortening the timetable to speed up implementation. We agreed, turning the seven-day plan into a two-day proposal. Q: Under the two-day plan, would the United States act on the first day and Iran on the second, with nuclear negotiations starting afterward?
​
No. The Americans would fulfill their commitments on the first day. On the second, we would reopen the Strait, and negotiations between Iran and the United States on a final agreement would begin. The talks were to start that day, not conclude then.
​
Under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, we had allowed 60 days for negotiations, with the possibility of an extension. The two-day plan set no deadline: talks would begin immediately and continue f . . .
